x: About this Hub A central place for the BW BricsCAD tool suite and the drafting practice behind it — built and maintained by the Western Sydney drafting team. The tools are for any office; the standards are ours, shared openly rather than imposed.

The first version of this toolset was written by Adrian Shaw in the drafting team, long before automating drafting work was widely considered part of the job. He automated the repetitive steps he kept running into — on his own, largely self-taught, with none of the tooling that makes this straightforward today. It began as a handful of routines that each saved a few minutes, and grew as more were added. Over time it became a large part of how efficiently the office drafted and how quickly survey plans could be turned around. He was early. Automating drafting work simply wasn't part of how the job was thought about yet, so for a long stretch it had no audience beyond his own desk — he kept at it because he could see what it would be worth once it was finished. Once it was, the office came with him, and people started bringing their own problems to it. He was ahead of his time, and everything here rests on what he started. Others across Western Sydney added to it over the years — drafters, surveyors and engineers who solved their own problem and shared the result. But those tools lived wherever they happened to be written: a routine on one person's desktop, a script passed around by email, a template on a network drive. They worked, and you only found them if someone showed you. This Hub is the result of collecting them. The routines were gathered, rewritten where needed, and packaged into a single BricsCAD suite with one installer — Adrian's original ported across command by command onto a modern platform, with the work that replaced it still crediting it throughout. The documentation was written alongside, directly against the shipping tools, so the pages describe how they actually behave. Collecting that work, building the installer and maintaining this site is the ongoing job of the Western Sydney Drafting department . The drafting floor at LPC House, Oran Park — where the suite is built and maintained.

The suite spans the disciplines that share the floor: Drafting — the WSY Drafting ribbon: cadastre, sheeting, annotation, boundary dimensioning and curve tables. Survey — the WAE ribbon for Works-As-Executed plans. Engineering — the BW Engineering ribbon: standard text heights, leaders, dimensions, scales and plotting. Office tools — the NSW Lot Loader and the Point Cloud Digitizer, which pull outside data into a drawing. Quality — the drawing checklist panel. Community LISP — well-regarded public routines the office has long relied on, bundled so they load with everything else instead of being installed by hand.

You're welcome here. Nothing here is limited to Western Sydney, and the installer is open to anyone at Beveridge Williams — take the whole suite or tick only the components you want, since each one works on its own. Be aware of what you're picking up, though. These tools were shaped by the work this office does: NSW cadastre, deposited and detail plans, Works-As-Executed surveys. The standards pages describe how Western Sydney draws, not a firm-wide mandate. Some of it will transfer unchanged, some will need adapting, and some won't suit you at all — that's expected.

The suite is still moving. If a command misbehaves, a page is wrong or out of date, or you have a routine of your own worth folding in, say so — that's how everything here got here in the first place. Head to Support & Requests and use the form there — a bug report, an idea, a tool you've built, or a question are all equally welcome, and it goes straight to the team. Annotation Annotation scales and cycling through them.

Creates annotation scales from a dialog, working out the ratio for you. Ribbon · Annotation → Create New Scale How to use it Opens a dialog. Enter the drawing units (the denominator — 200 for 1:200) and a name. The ▾ menu inserts sequence tokens so you can create a run of scales at once: {1-5} — numbers, so Sheet {1-5} makes Sheet 1 … Sheet 5 {01-10} — zero-padded numbers {A-E} — letters Queue scales with + ; they're all created when you close the dialog. What it produces Named annotation scales using the office convention for metre drawings — 1:200 becomes paper 1, drawing 0.2. Note — This is the same tool on the BW Engineering ribbon, and builds the named per-lot scales that SETLAYOUT and INCBLOCK rely on.

Step forward or back through the drawing's annotation scales. Ribbon · Annotation → Next Scale / Previous Scale How to use it No prompts. The new scale is reported on the command line, and the list wraps at both ends. Note — Scales imported from xrefs are skipped, so cycling stays within the drawing's own list. Previous Command Reference
Cadastre Boundaries, lot numbers, areas, bearings, easements and roads.

These all work the same way. Select text first and it's restyled in place — single-line text is converted to MText. Run with nothing selected and it loops, prompting Text insertion point [ESC to exit]: and opening the text editor at each point until you press Esc. Command Places Text style Layer SUBLN Subject lot number LARGE LABEL SUB DP SUBA Subject lot area MEDIUM LABEL SUB AREA SUBD Lot dimension text SMALL LABEL SUB DIMENSIONS SUBB Bearing and distance SMALL LABEL SUB BEARINGS ADJLN Adjoining lot number ADJOINING LABEL ADJ DP ROADN Road name LARGE LABEL ROAD NAME ROADL Road label THIN LABEL ROAD LABEL EASET Easement text THIN LABEL EASEMENT LABEL Note — text height is the drawing's TEXTSIZE divided by the current annotation scale, and everything is created annotative. Set the right annotation scale before you place text.

Moves lot boundary lines onto the subject-boundary layer, or traces a new boundary. Ribbon · Cadastre → Subject Boundary How to use it Select the boundary lines first, then run the command — they move straight to the layer with no further prompts. Run it with nothing selected and it hands off to the native -BOUNDARY command so you can pick internal points. What it produces Layer SUB BDY (cyan). Selected lines are replaced by two-vertex polylines; existing polylines are kept. Colour, linetype and lineweight are set ByLayer. Note — Only lines and polylines are affected; anything else in the selection is left alone.

The same thing for adjoining lots. Ribbon · Cadastre → Adjoining Boundary How to use it Works exactly like SUBBDY — pre-select the lines to move them, or run with nothing selected to trace with -BOUNDARY . What it produces Layer ADJ BDY (white).

Draws or converts easement outlines on the dashed easement layer. Ribbon · Cadastre → Easement Area How to use it Pre-select easement outlines to convert them, or run with nothing selected to trace a new outline with -BOUNDARY . What it produces Layer EASEMENT (green, DASHED), drawn at a 0.25 linetype scale so the dashes read at plan scale. Note — Needs the DASHED linetype loaded in the drawing.

Draws easement boundary lines by hand. Ribbon · Cadastre → Easement Lines How to use it Runs the native PLINE command on the easement layer — draw as normal. What it produces Layer EASEMENT , with the condensed linetype scale applied while drawing.

Places an easement dimension arrow between two snapped points. Ribbon · Cadastre → Easement Arrow How to use it Runs DIMALIGNED — pick the two points to dimension between. Intersection and insertion snaps are forced on while it runs. What it produces Layer EASEMENT LABEL using the EASEMENT LABEL dimension style. Note — Your running object snaps are overridden while the command runs, then restored.

Easement label leader — a spline leader with a dot arrowhead. Ribbon · Cadastre → Easement Marker How to use it Runs the native MLEADER command — place the leader as normal. What it produces Layer EASEMENT LABEL , text style THIN LABEL.

Stacks one text neatly under another at a fixed gap — typically an area under a lot number. Ribbon · Cadastre → Align Area How to use it Prompts Enter offset value <2.0>: (the last value you used), then loops: Select the anchor text: → Select text to align with anchor: . The second text is moved below the first. Esc exits. What it produces Moves existing text; creates nothing. The gap accounts for both text heights plus your offset, scaled by the annotation scale. Note — Only text and mtext are accepted. The offset value is remembered for the rest of the session.

Splits a bearing into three separate texts — degrees, minutes and seconds — so each can sit over its own boundary segment. Ribbon · Cadastre → Stretch Bearing How to use it Prompts Enter input method [Manual/Select]: . Manual — asks for degrees, minutes and seconds in turn. Select — pick an existing bearing text; it's parsed and erased . You then drag-align each piece onto a curve in turn: degrees, then minutes, then seconds. What it produces Three MText labels, style SMALL LABEL on layer SUB BEARINGS .

The reverse of STRETCHB — merges three split bearing texts back into one label on a curve. Ribbon · Cadastre → Condense Bearing How to use it Prompts for the degrees, minutes and seconds texts in turn. All three are erased and their contents joined, then you drag-align the combined label onto a curve. What it produces One MText, style SMALL LABEL on SUB BEARINGS . Watch out — The three source texts are erased before you place the new label. If you cancel the placement, press U once to get them back.

Measures a road width between two points and writes (X.XX WIDE) at the midpoint. Ribbon · Cadastre → Road Label (Measured) How to use it First point: → Second point: , with perpendicular and nearest snaps forced on. What it produces MText on layer ROAD LABEL , rotated to run across the road and flipped if needed to stay readable. Note — Single shot — it doesn't loop. Previous Command Reference
Commands without a ribbon button Typed at the command line - a large part of the toolset, including the whole boundary dimensioning and curve table workflow.

These commands are designed to run in sequence: AUTODIM dimensions every boundary segment and drops a numbered label on each curve. DIMRENUM tidies the numbering if you've edited things. CURVETABLE builds a schedule from those numbered labels. CURVETABLEUPDATE resyncs the table after further edits.

FILL1 through FILL11 hatch earthworks depth bands. Each sets its layer then runs a solid hatch behind the boundary, repeating until you press Esc — so you can hatch many lots in one band without re-running. Command Depth band FILL1 0.0 – 0.5 FILL2 0.5 – 1.0 FILL3 1.0 – 1.5 FILL4 1.5 – 2.0 FILL5 2.0 – 2.5 FILL6 2.5 – 3.0 FILL7 Over 3 FILL8 4 FILL9 5 FILL10 6 FILL11 7 Note — none of the fill commands has a ribbon button.

Shows or hides annotative objects at all scales, not just the current one. How to use it No prompts — it's a toggle, and reports the new state. Note — Useful for checking what's attached to which scale. No ribbon button.

Dimensions every segment of the selected lot boundaries in one hit — length inside, bearing outside, and a numbered label on each curve. How to use it Pre-select, or Select polylines/arcs: . Then Enter precision <3>: → Include bearings? [Yes/No] <Yes>: → Starting curve number: (defaults to this drawing's highest existing label plus one). What it produces Lengths on SUB DIMENSIONS , bearings on SUB BEARINGS , and a numbered curve label on DIM LABEL for each arc — the labels the curve table is built from. Note — Re-running is safe: existing labels aren't doubled up, so it only fills in what's missing, and a boundary shared between two lots is dimensioned once. If a segment can't be dimensioned it's reported on the command line rather than skipped silently.

Places numbered dimension-label bubbles, or converts existing text into them. How to use it Pre-select text to convert it. Otherwise Specify starting number: then place them one at a time; the number increments as you go. What it produces Dimension Label blocks on DIM LABEL . Note — Numbering carries on from the highest number already in the drawing, skipping any that's taken.

Renumbers dimension labels in sequence, closing gaps left by deleted ones. How to use it Pre-select, or Select dimension labels to renumber: → Starting number <1>: . The select prompt also offers Sequence , which decides what order the numbers go in. Sequence Existing — keeps the order already on the labels and just closes the gaps left by deleted ones. This is what the command has always done. Reading — renumbers top-down and then left-to-right, the way you read the sheet. Use it when the numbering has drifted out of step with the drawing. Note — Your choice is remembered between sessions, and the command says which order it used. Reading order groups labels into rows by height band rather than comparing exactly, so two labels a whisker apart still count as the same row instead of one jumping the queue.

Builds a schedule of curved dimensions from the numbered curve labels, or exports them to CSV. How to use it In model space: pre-select, or Select dimension label blocks or Enter for all: . In a layout: it asks you to Select viewport(s): and includes only the labels visible in them. You can pick several — one at a time, by dragging a window across the sheet, or by selecting them before you run the command — so a layout with an overall and a couple of detail blow-ups gets one combined schedule instead of a table each. Either the viewport or its clip boundary works. Then N curves — specify table insertion point or [Export]: . Export writes a CSV. What it produces A table titled Schedule of Short & Curved Dimensions on the TEXT layer, with columns for number, bearing, chord, arc and radius, sorted numerically. Note — In a layout it lists only the curves actually visible in the viewports you pick, and a curve showing in two of them is listed once rather than twice. If none qualify, it tells you why on the command line. Keeping it current — CURVETABLEUPDATE resyncs a placed table from every viewport it was built from. Delete one of them later and the table simply shrinks on the next update; it only loses its link when every source viewport is gone.

Resyncs a placed curve table with the drawing — adds new curves, drops deleted ones, refreshes changed values. How to use it Select curve table to update or Enter to refresh all: . Note — Only works on tables created by CURVETABLE. The table keeps the size it was created at, so it won't jump around if you've changed annotation scale.

Turns live curve-table refreshing on or off. How to use it A toggle — no prompts. The setting is remembered between sessions. Note — On by default, so a placed curve table keeps itself current as you edit the labels it's built from. Turn it off if the redraw gets in the way on a heavy sheet.

The inverse of CURVETABLE — reads a hand-drawn or imported curve schedule and writes its values back into the matching numbered labels. How to use it Pre-select, or Select the curve schedule text (window the whole table): . What it reads Three shapes of source data, including a table that mixes them: A cell per text object — the older export, one piece of text per value. A whole row in one line — the newer export, columns separated by spaces. Bearings written with spaces ( 128° 05' 12" ) stay in one piece, and the AutoCAD %%d degree code is understood. Values annotated beside the curve — not a table at all, but separate text on the plan: 81°48'10" , C6.685 , A6.775 , R12.070 . Select them and DIMDATA replaces them with a proper numbered dimension label where the text was. C is the chord, A (or L ) the arc, R the radius, and anything with degree marks is the bearing; lower case and an optional space or = are accepted. Where the arc and chord are equal and the plan writes them once as A&C6.685 , both are filled from it. Bearings with the seconds left off ( 81°48' ) are read too, and the missing seconds written in as 00" so one sheet does not end up with two formats. Note — The column order is read from the header, not assumed. A schedule headed No / Bearing / Distance / Radius / Arc holds the same data in a different order, and taking it at face value would write every radius into the arc and every arc into the radius — which looks entirely plausible on a plan. DISTANCE is understood as the chord, ARC LENGTH as the arc and CHORD BEARING as the bearing. Note — Anything it cannot read stops it rather than letting it guess, so an ordinary selection of text is never mistaken for curve data.

Joins a tree's scattered annotation — spread, diameter, height and tree number, each its own piece of text — into one mtext, leaving the spot level exactly where it is. How to use it Pre-select, or Select the tree annotation text (window the lot of it): — window whole clusters, as many trees as you like in one go. Each tree becomes one label, starting on the point its first text started: S:4 D:0.2 H:5 No:3 What it reads S , D and H with a value, however punctuated — S: 4 , S4 , s 4 all read. Measurements must be numbers. The tree number as No , No. or N — and it may be 3a or 12B , since split trees happen. Values are kept exactly as the surveyor wrote them — 0.20 stays 0.20 , because the trailing zero is a statement about precision. The order is whatever the drawing has. H D S is written back as H D S , judged along the line of text so rotated annotation reads correctly too. What it produces One mtext per tree — measurements on the first line, the number below — matching the text it replaces for layer, style, height, colour and rotation. The source text is erased in the same step, so one undo takes the whole change back. Note — Spot levels are never touched. They carry no tag, so the command simply cannot pick them up. Note — A tree needs its three measurements; the number is optional — unnumbered trees are joined the same and just have no second line, and one never borrows its neighbour's number. Where two trees' text has run together (the same tag twice in one cluster) it says so and leaves them alone — do those few one tree at a time.

Places a schedule of the easements the chosen viewport(s) can actually show — e.g. (A1) EASEMENT TO DRAIN WATER 3 WIDE , one line per designation. How to use it Run it on a layout tab (on Model it tells you to switch — the schedule belongs on the sheet). Select viewport(s) for the schedule: — pick one, or as many as you like by picking them in turn, dragging a window over the sheet, or selecting them before you run the command. Either the viewport or its clip boundary works. One viewport scopes the schedule to that viewport, which is usually what a detail wants; several give one combined schedule for the sheet, and an easement showing in two of them is listed once. Then → a dialog lists every designation found and you word each one: pick a standard description, take the suggestion the code letters offer (label an easement (A1) and it proposes EASEMENT TO DRAIN WATER — one click, then type the width), or type your own. Create stays greyed until every designation has wording — the button counts down what's left. Then Schedule insertion point: . What it produces A text schedule on the sheet, always in CAPITALS, linked to its viewport. It reads designations from the EASEMENT LABEL layer, so labels placed with EASET , EASEP and EASEARROW all count. A sheet with two details lists only what each viewport shows. The wording is stored in the drawing itself, so a re-issued plan reproduces exactly as drawn. You can't type into a schedule — it's generated text, so a hand edit is undone and the schedule goes back to saying what the drawing says. Change the wording with EASEDESC instead. If nothing's found, the command says why — how many labels it checked, and how many were at another annotation scale, outside the view, or unlabelled. No ribbon button.

Resyncs every placed easement schedule with the drawing. How to use it No prompts — it refreshes all schedules and reports how many changed. Note — with EASELEGAUTO on (the default) you'll rarely need it; it's the manual catch-up for when tracking has been turned off. Note — a schedule built from several viewports refreshes from all of them. Delete one of those viewports later and the schedule simply shrinks on the next refresh; it only stops tracking when every viewport it was built from is gone.

Turns live easement-schedule tracking on or off. How to use it A toggle — no prompts. The setting is remembered between sessions. Note — On by default: schedules follow the drawing as you lay a sheet out, so one is never quietly stale. Turn it off if the redraw gets in the way on a heavy sheet.

Words the drawing's easements without placing or touching a schedule. How to use it The same wording dialog as EASELEG, but covering the whole drawing rather than one viewport — so you can describe an easement before the sheet that shows it exists, or fix a description later without placing anything. Placed schedules pick the change up straight away. Note — designations you've worded before stay editable here even if their label has since been deleted, so a stale entry can always be corrected.

Opens your personal easement description list for editing. How to use it No prompts — the list opens in Notepad. One description per line; save, and it's offered next time. Note — the office standard set (with its code-letter suggestions) ships with the suite; your own additions merge over it. EASEDB edits your personal suggestion list — EASEDESC edits what a particular drawing says.

Places adjoining-lot text in the office's adjoining style. How to use it Sets the ADJOINING LABEL style and the text layer, then places text the usual way. Note — the adjoining sibling of the lot-text commands. No ribbon button.

An aligned dimension for house measurements, with the value in parentheses. How to use it Places an aligned dimension; the measurement is written as (12.34) . What it produces An annotative dimension in the HOUSE DIMENSION style (SMALL LABEL text), created if the drawing doesn't have it. Note — No ribbon button.
An aligned dimension prefixed SETBACK . How to use it Same as HDIM, but the measurement reads SETBACK 6.00 . What it produces An annotative dimension in the SETBACK style. Note — No ribbon button.

Wall-to-boundary: measures between two points and labels the distance along the line. How to use it First point: → Second point: . Perpendicular and nearest snaps are turned on for the picks and restored afterwards. What it produces Text reading Wall to / Bdy X.XX at the midpoint of the measured line, rounded to the nearest 0.005, in SMALL LABEL on the text layer. Note — No ribbon button.

Moves objects to the non-plotting layer. How to use it Pre-select and it moves them all at once; otherwise select when asked. What it produces The selection lands on NO PLOT with properties ByLayer — visible on screen, absent from the plot. Note — Handy for construction lines and working notes. No ribbon button.

Rounds bearings in selected text to the nearest 5 seconds — the office survey convention. How to use it Pre-select, or Select bearing text to round: . Works on both text and mtext. Note — Understands both the ° character and the %%d degree code, and writes back whichever the text already used. No ribbon button.

Labels each selected lot with its area. How to use it Pre-select, or Select polylines to label: . The select prompt also offers Placement , which decides where in the lot the label lands. What it produces Area labels on SUB AREA , placed inside each lot. Areas read in m² below a hectare and ha above. Placement The same four options are on MTC , and your choice is remembered between sessions. Fit (the default) — the best spot for the size of this label. A label is a wide rectangle, so on a lot wider than it is deep the roomiest point can still let it overhang the frontage; this finds where it actually fits. Roomiest — the point furthest from every boundary. Centre — the true centroid of the lot. Box — the centre of the extents. Predictable, and it lines labels up neatly across a row of similar lots. Note — Every mode falls back to Roomiest rather than putting a label outside the lot: a centroid lands outside an L-shaped lot, and a long label may fit nowhere.

Builds a complete set of per-lot sales layouts — one sheet per lot, each centred and scaled to its own lot. How to use it Select the viewport in your MAIN sales layout: → Enter plot scale denominator (e.g. 200 for 1:200) <200>: . Everything else is automatic. What it produces One annotation scale and one layout per lot, each viewport centred on its lot. Tabs are sorted into lot order. Note — Lot numbers are read as text on the SUB DP layer, so a missing or mis-layered lot number simply won't get a sheet — which makes this a handy QA pass. Pair with INCBLOCK. No ribbon button.

Turns each lot into a numbered annotative block that's only visible at its own scale. How to use it Enter starting block number <next free number>: then loop: Select lot to block as "N" <exit>: . The annotation scale advances after each lot. What it produces A block named after each number containing a copy of the lot, referenced on SUB BDY . Note — The original lot is left untouched — a copy becomes the block content. Create the named per-lot scales first with CSCALE. No ribbon button.

Adds a prefix or suffix to selected text. How to use it Add text as [Prefix/Suffix] <Suffix>: → Text to add: . Pre-select, or you'll be asked to select afterwards. Note — Dimensions keep their live measured value, as with TBRK.

Writes surface levels into existing text by picking points. How to use it Picks an elevation source first, then loops: Select text: → Select point for level: . What it produces Overwrites the picked text with the elevation to one decimal place. Note — Samples from the drawing's TIN surface, or 3D faces if there's no TIN — so your pick only needs to be right in plan, not snapped to 3D geometry. No ribbon button.

Offsets a whole selection at once, with a live preview, repeating until you stop. How to use it Specify offset distance or [Through/Erase]: — Erase asks whether to delete the sources, Through takes the distance from the cursor. Then select objects and drag to choose the side. Note — A whole batch offsets consistently — closed shapes all grow or all shrink together. You can type an exact distance mid-drag.
Copies blocks or text to every vertex of the chosen polylines. How to use it Pre-select the objects to copy, or you'll be asked. Then Base point: → Select target polylines: .

Turns polylines into pipes — a styled centreline with two wall lines that follow it when you edit. How to use it Pre-select, or Select polylines to convert to pipes: → Enter pipe size: . Note — Edit the centreline and the walls follow; they're locked so they can't be dragged off. The last pipe size is remembered between sessions.

Imports an NSW ePlan / LandXML file — lot boundaries, lot numbers with areas, and monument labels. How to use it Opens a file dialog, then Import CgPoints as point entities? [Yes/No] <No>: . What it produces Boundaries on the subject or adjoining layers by parcel class, with labels on the matching text layers. Arcs are preserved. Note — Wide arcs (sweeping over 180°) are flagged on the command line so you can check them against the plan.
Chops decimals off the number in selected text — cutting, not rounding. How to use it Pre-select, then Decimal places <2>: . Note — Only the first number in the text is affected.
Rounds the number in selected text — up, down or to nearest. How to use it Rounding mode [Nearest/Up/Down]: → Decimal places <2>: . Note — The rounding mode is remembered between uses.

Fills in title-block attributes across all layouts from a central CSV register. How to use it No prompts — it runs from files. Note — Needs a _DWGLISTCSV.TXT file beside the drawing whose first line names the CSV register. The CSV has the drawing name in the first column, layout name in the second, and attribute tags as the remaining headers.
Turns closed shapes into wipeouts. How to use it Pre-select or select circles, ellipses and polylines, then Do you want to keep the original entities? [Yes/No] <Yes>: .

Strips all inline formatting out of text, leaving the plain words. How to use it Pre-select, or select mtext, leaders, dimensions or blocks with attributes. Note — Line breaks are kept. Background masks aren't touched — use TBG for those.

Bulk layer rename — add or remove a prefix or suffix, or find-and-replace, across many layers at once. How to use it Bulk layer rename — operation: [AddPrefix/AddSuffix/RemovePrefix/RemoveSuffix/Replace] → the text to add, remove or find (Replace also asks Replace with (blank to delete it): ) → Apply to layers matching <*>: — a wildcard filter, so SURV* touches only the survey layers. Note — layer 0 and xref layers are always skipped, and a rename that would collide with an existing name is skipped and reported rather than failing the run. No ribbon button.

Normalises the entities inside blocks to layer 0 / ByBlock, so the insert's own layer and properties control how the block looks. How to use it Pre-select block references, or Blocks to normalise [Select/All] <Select>: ( All covers every block definition in the drawing) → Also change entities in nested blocks? [Yes/No] <Yes>: . What it produces Every entity inside the chosen block definitions moves to layer 0 with colour, linetype and lineweight set to ByBlock — from then on, changing the insert changes the block. Note — dynamic blocks are handled through their real definition, so the change survives parameter edits. Xrefs are left alone. Every insert of an edited definition is affected — it changes the block, not one insert. No ribbon button.

Checks for a newer release of the suite and launches the installer. How to use it If an update exists: Update to vX? BricsCAD will need to close to finish. [Yes/No] <Yes>: . Previous Command Reference
Occupations Fences, walls and other occupations shown against a boundary.

Draws an occupation fence line using the fence linetype. Ribbon · Occupations → Fence How to use it Runs the native MLEADER command — draw the fence line as normal. What it produces Layer SURV OCCS with the Fence linetype. Note — Needs the Support linetype file. If the fence draws solid, the linetype didn't load — see Troubleshooting.

Boundary fence tick line. Ribbon · Occupations → Fence Ticks How to use it Runs the native MLEADER command, with endpoint and nearest snaps forced on. What it produces Layer SURV OCCS with the Fence Tick linetype.

Inserts a wall symbol at a point and rotation. Ribbon · Occupations → Wall How to use it Specify insertion point: → Specify rotation <0>: . What it produces Wall blocks on SURV OCCS , annotative. Previous Command Reference

QA The drawing checklist panel. The QA panel holds a single button. The checklist itself — revisions, the automatic checks and saving a completed pass — is documented under Quality › Drawing Checklist .

Opens the project's drawing checklist — the NSW drafting QA form — for the drawing you have open. If the project doesn't have one yet, a copy is made from the master template bundled with the tool. The checklist lives two folders up from the drawing, in a 4 Checklists folder, matching the office project layout. The window is modeless so you can work in the drawing while it's open, and only one is live at a time. How to use it No prompts — run it and the checklist window opens. Warnings appear as message boxes: the drawing not being saved yet, or the bundled master template being missing. What it produces Nothing in the drawing. It opens (or creates) Drafting - Drawing Checklist NSW SUR-FO-0615 v1.0.xlsx in the project's 4 Checklists folder. Note — The button for this sits on the WSY Drafting ribbon's QA panel — there is no button for it on the Engineering, WAE or WSY Tools tabs. Closing a saved drawing that has a project checklist prompts you to complete it first; answering yes opens the checklist modally and holds the close until you're done. Previous Command Reference

Setout & Ident Setback, building tie and height dimension tools. Not documented — these commands ship on the ribbon but don't have reference entries yet. Commands on this panel: HDIM , SETBACK , WTB . Previous Command Reference
Sheeting North points and sheet set loading.

Drops a north point already rotated to match a viewport's twist. Ribbon · Sheeting → North Point How to use it Select viewport: — then a live preview follows your cursor; click to place. Esc cancels. What it produces A North Point block on layer NORTH , annotative, rotated to the viewport's twist angle. Note — You can pick the viewport's clip boundary instead of its edge — either resolves to the owning viewport.

Opens this drawing's sheet set, or offers to build one if it doesn't exist. Ribbon · Sheeting → Sheet Set How to use it If a matching .dst sits beside the drawing it opens and saves. Otherwise: No sheet set found for this drawing (name.dst). Create one? [Yes/No] <Yes>: — on Yes it picks a template, adds every paper layout as a sheet, and opens the result. What it produces A sheet set named after the drawing, in the drawing's folder. Note — Requires a saved drawing with at least one paper layout. The template is chosen from the drawing's filename suffix — DP/SP/CP/PP use the plan form template, SET/ID/FW/PEG the setout template, SAL/LOT the lot template, anything else the detail template. Opens the drafting documentation in your browser — the ribbon's Help button. How to use it No prompts. If the browser can't be opened it says so on the command line.

Survey Pegs, reference marks, SSMs, ties and traverse lines.

These follow the same pattern as the cadastre text commands — pre-select to restyle, or run with nothing selected to place new text in a loop. Command Places Layer REFT Reference mark text SURV REFERENCE TEXT TIET Ties text SURV TIES TEXT SSMT SSM / MGA text SURV SSM TEXT TRAVT Traverse text SURV TRAVERSE TEXT OCCST Occupations text SURV OCCS TEXT

Drops peg symbols, either one at a time or on every vertex of chosen polylines. Ribbon · Survey → Peg How to use it Select polylines first and a peg is placed on every vertex. Otherwise: Specify insertion point or [Place]: — pick points one at a time, or type Place to select polylines instead. Endpoint snap is forced on. What it produces Peg blocks on layer PEG , annotative and attached to the current scale. Note — Vertex mode skips any vertex that already has a block, so re-running is safe.

Places reference marks, or swaps existing blocks for reference marks in place. Ribbon · Survey → Reference Mark How to use it Specify insertion point or [Replace]: . Replace loops asking for blocks to swap; each is erased and a reference mark inserted at its position. What it produces Reference Mark blocks on SURV REFERENCE , annotative. Note — Replace keeps only the position — the old block's rotation and attributes are dropped.

Places SSM (state survey mark) symbols in a loop. Ribbon · Survey → SSM How to use it Loops Specify insertion point: until you press Enter or Esc. What it produces SSM blocks on SURV SSM MARK , annotative.

Place a single 'X' or 'Y' mark symbol. Ribbon · Survey → 'X' Symbol / 'Y' Symbol How to use it One prompt: Specify insertion point: . Single shot — these don't repeat. What it produces X or Y blocks on SURV SSM MARK .

Draws a tie line between two points, labelling the distance on one side and the bearing on the other. Ribbon · Survey → Ties How to use it Specify base point for leader: → Specify second point for leader: , with endpoint, intersection and perpendicular snaps forced on. What it produces A dashed leader on SURV TIES plus two labels on SURV TIES TEXT — distance one side, bearing the other. Distance is rounded to the nearest 0.005; the bearing reads to the nearest 5 seconds.

Draws a traverse line — a dashed annotative leader with no text. Ribbon · Survey → Traverse How to use it Runs the native MLEADER command. What it produces Layer SURV TRAVERSE with the condensed linetype scale. Previous Command Reference
Text Text styles, leaders, brackets, masks and curve-aligned labels.

Pre-select text to restyle it, or run with nothing selected to place new text in a loop. All four place on the TEXT layer. Command Style THINTXT THIN LABEL SMALLTXT SMALL LABEL MEDTXT MEDIUM LABEL LRGTXT LARGE LABEL

Label leaders — straight-segment or spline — whose text matches your current style. Ribbon · Text → Straight Leader / Curved Leader How to use it Both run the native MLEADER command. What it produces The leader takes your current text style and height, so it matches surrounding annotation.

Aligns text along a curve with a live drag preview. Ribbon · Text → Align Text to Curve How to use it Select text to align [New/Settings] <Exit>: — pick existing text, type New to type fresh text, or Settings to open the options dialog. Then pick the curve or multileader to align to, and drag into position. While dragging: + / - step the offset, < / > rotate, Y toggles readability, B toggles the background mask, O and R prompt for exact values. What it produces Aligns the picked text, or creates new text using the layer and style set in Settings. Note — Settings has a Multiple mode that keeps placing copies down a line, and a Copy mode that leaves the original in place. Settings persist between sessions and are shared with CLABEL.

Type a phrase and drag each word onto a curve in turn. Ribbon · Text → Align Custom Label How to use it Enter label words (space-separated): then drag each word onto a curve. The word list wraps, so you can keep going along a fence line. What it produces Text created with the shared ATC settings — on the layer and style those settings specify.

Drops each selected label into the middle of its lot. Ribbon · Text → Move to Center How to use it Pre-select, or Select closed polylines and text: . Each label moves to the middle of the nearest lot that hasn't already taken a label. The select prompt also offers Placement , which decides what “the middle” means. What it produces Moves existing mtext; creates nothing. Placement The same four options are on ALAB , and your choice is remembered between sessions. Fit (the default) — the best spot for the size of this label, so a wide label on a shallow lot does not overhang the frontage. Roomiest — the point furthest from every boundary. Centre — the true centroid. Box — the centre of the extents; predictable, and it lines labels up across a row of similar lots. Note — The label lands inside the lot, even on concave or L-shaped ones: every mode falls back to Roomiest rather than placing a label outside the boundary.

Adds or removes brackets around selected text. Ribbon · Text → Toggle Brackets How to use it Pre-select, or select text, mtext, leaders or dimensions. Each is toggled individually. Note — Dimensions keep their live measured value.

Turns background masks on or off behind selected text. Ribbon · Text → Toggle Background Mask How to use it Pre-select mtext, leaders or dimensions to toggle immediately, or run and use the Settings keyword to set the mask scale and colour first. Note — Settings masks with the drawing background, a fixed colour, or Auto , which matches the colour of the hatch behind each label. Changing any setting turns the mask on rather than toggling it. Topography Batters and contour labelling.

Fills the space between a top and toe line with batter ticks, each stretched to span the gap. Ribbon · Topography → Batter How to use it Select top batter curve: → Select toe (bottom) batter curve: → then drag to set the tick spacing, with the whole run previewing live. Click to confirm, Esc to cancel. What it produces Batter blocks on the BATTER layer, each rotated toward the toe and scaled to span the local gap. Note — Spacing is adaptive — ticks crowd where the batter narrows. Works on 3D top and toe strings, though the output lands flat.

Labels a contour with its elevation, sitting the text on the line with a mask through it. Ribbon · Topography → Contour Label How to use it Loops: Select contour <exit>: then drag the label along it. Enter or Esc exits. What it produces Masked annotative text on your current layer and style, sitting on the contour so the mask reads. Note — The elevation comes from the contour's start point. Annotation BW standard text heights, matching multileaders and the dimension wrappers.

The smallest of the four BW text heights, for general notes and callouts on engineering plans. Like the rest of the family it does double duty: it places new text, and it reformats text you already have to the standard. How to use it Select the text first and it's reformatted in place — single-line text is converted to MText on the way. Run it with nothing selected and it loops, prompting Text insertion point [ESC to exit] and opening the in-place editor at each point until you press Esc. Empty results are discarded. What it produces Annotative MText in the BW_AN style on layer T25 (yellow), colour ByLayer, line spacing 0.8 at-least. The height is the drawing's TEXTSIZE — set to 2.5 by this command — divided by the current annotation scale value. Reformatted text is attached middle-centre; newly placed text is attached top-left. Note — Set the right annotation scale before you place text — the height is derived from it.

The 3.5 mm step of the BW text family — the usual choice for sub-headings and labels that need to read above general note text. How to use it Select the text first and it's reformatted in place — single-line text is converted to MText on the way. Run it with nothing selected and it loops, prompting Text insertion point [ESC to exit] and opening the in-place editor at each point until you press Esc. What it produces Annotative MText in the BW_AN style on layer T35 (green), at a working TEXTSIZE of 3.5 divided by the current annotation scale value.

The 5 mm step of the BW text family, for headings and anything that has to stand out on a plotted sheet. How to use it Select the text first and it's reformatted in place — single-line text is converted to MText on the way. Run it with nothing selected and it loops, prompting Text insertion point [ESC to exit] until you press Esc. What it produces Annotative MText in the BW_AN style on layer T50 (cyan), at a working TEXTSIZE of 5.0 divided by the current annotation scale value.

The largest of the four BW text heights — plan titles and major headings. How to use it Select the text first and it's reformatted in place — single-line text is converted to MText on the way. Run it with nothing selected and it loops, prompting Text insertion point [ESC to exit] until you press Esc. What it produces Annotative MText in the BW_AN style on layer T70 (blue), at a working TEXTSIZE of 7.0 divided by the current annotation scale value.

The aligned equivalent of BWDIMLIN — the dimension line runs parallel to the two points rather than orthogonally. How to use it Run the command and the native DIMALIGNED prompts follow — pick the two points, then place the dimension line. What it produces An aligned dimension on layer DIMS in the BWAN_DIM25 style.

Dimensions the angle between two lines, or the included angle of an arc or circle, with the BW layer and style already set. How to use it Run the command and the native DIMANGULAR prompts follow — pick the two lines (or the arc), then place the dimension arc. What it produces An angular dimension on layer DIMS in the BWAN_DIM25 style. Angular decimal places are set to 0 in that style.

Dimensions the length along an arc rather than the chord — used on kerb returns and curved alignments. How to use it Run the command and the native DIMARC prompts follow — select the arc or polyline arc segment, then place the dimension. What it produces An arc length dimension on layer DIMS in the BWAN_DIM25 style.

Labels the diameter of a circle or arc — typically pipes and pits — with the BW layer and dimension style already set. How to use it Run the command and the native DIMDIAMETER prompts follow — select the circle or arc, then place the dimension text. What it produces A diameter dimension on layer DIMS in the BWAN_DIM25 style.

A wrapper around the native DIMLINEAR that sets the DIMS layer and the BW dimension style first, so you never have to remember to switch either. How to use it Run the command and the normal linear dimension prompts follow — pick the two extension line origins, then place the dimension line. What it produces A linear dimension on layer DIMS (white) in the BWAN_DIM25 style: 2.5 mm yellow text in BW_AN, 2.5 mm closed filled arrows, two decimal places, text above the dimension line, and annotative.

Labels the radius of a circle or arc with the BW layer and dimension style already set. How to use it Run the command and the native DIMRADIUS prompts follow — select the circle or arc, then place the dimension text. What it produces A radius dimension on layer DIMS in the BWAN_DIM25 style.

Places a multileader whose text height, arrow size and dogleg all match the 2.5 mm BW text standard, so a leader note sits alongside BW25 text without looking out of scale. How to use it Run the command and the native MLEADER takes over — pick the arrow point, then the landing, then type the text. What it produces A multileader on layer T25 using the BWAN_ML25 style: straight leader, dogleg enabled at 2.5, 2.5 mm arrow, annotative MText content in BW_AN at 2.5 mm, leader and text colour ByLayer, landing gap 1.5, attached to the middle of the top line and held horizontal. The style is made current ( CMLEADERSTYLE ).

The 3.5 mm multileader, sized to sit with BW35 text. How to use it Run the command and the native MLEADER takes over — pick the arrow point, then the landing, then type the text. What it produces A multileader on layer T35 using the BWAN_ML35 style — same specification as the rest of the family, with the text height, arrow size and dogleg length all at 3.5.

The 5 mm multileader, sized to sit with BW50 text. How to use it Run the command and the native MLEADER takes over — pick the arrow point, then the landing, then type the text. What it produces A multileader on layer T50 using the BWAN_ML50 style, with the text height, arrow size and dogleg length all at 5.0.

The largest BW multileader, sized to sit with BW70 text. How to use it Run the command and the native MLEADER takes over — pick the arrow point, then the landing, then type the text. What it produces A multileader on layer T70 using the BWAN_ML70 style, with the text height, arrow size and dogleg length all at 7.0. Previous Command Reference
Open Titleblock update, the drawing register and the job folder.

Opens the folder the active drawing lives in — handy for grabbing a reference, checking the rasters folder or dropping a PDF next to the DWG. How to use it No prompts — run it and Explorer opens at the drawing's folder. What it produces Nothing in the drawing. Note — The drawing has to have been saved; an unsaved drawing has no folder and you'll get Drawing folder not found (unsaved drawing?).

A shortcut to the register that sits beside the drawings, so you don't have to go looking for it in Explorer. How to use it No prompts — run it and the register opens. It looks in the current drawing's folder for the first file matching *_Drawing_Register.xls* , so both .xls and .xlsx registers are found. What it produces Nothing in the drawing — it opens the spreadsheet in whatever application is registered for it. Note — The drawing has to have been saved. If the folder can't be resolved you get Drawing folder not found (unsaved drawing?). , and if there's no register beside it, File not found.

Fills in every title block in the drawing from a shared CSV, so a project's sheet numbers, titles, dates and revisions are maintained in one spreadsheet rather than sheet by sheet. The drawing folder holds a pointer file, _DWGLISTCSV.TXT , whose first line names the CSV. In the CSV the first column is the drawing name, the second is the layout, and every remaining column heading is an attribute tag. How to use it No prompts — run it and it reports either --> Attributes are up-to-date. or --> N attributes updated in N blocks. Everything else it has to say is a diagnostic: the pointer file being missing or empty, the CSV not being found, the file not being a .csv , or this drawing's name not appearing in the first column. What it produces Changes attribute values on block references in the layouts named in the CSV. Only attributes whose tag matches a column heading and whose value actually differs are touched; nothing is created or erased. Note — Drawing names and layout names are matched case-insensitively, and the drawing name is compared without its extension. The CSV is read using the machine's regional list separator, falling back to a comma. Previous Command Reference
Plotting A1 and A3 PDF output, and A3 printing.

One-click PDF of the sheet you're looking at, at full A1 size. It drives the native -PLOT command with a fixed token stream, so there is nothing to set up and nothing to get wrong. How to use it Open the layout you want and run the command — there are no prompts. When the plot finishes the PDF is opened for you. What it produces A PDF written to your Documents folder, named drawing-layout.pdf after the drawing and the current layout, plotted through Print as PDF.pc3 on A1 media, millimetres, landscape, extents, centred, at 1:1. Note — Paper space only — in model space it says This function can only be used in paper space. and stops. If the Print as PDF.pc3 device isn't installed it refuses to start rather than half-plotting, and tells you to reinstall the suite. If you cancel the plot, or the PDF doesn't appear where it was expected, it says so on the command line instead of opening anything.

The half-size check print of the same sheet — an A1 layout reduced to A3. Used for markups and issue copies. How to use it Open the layout you want and run the command — there are no prompts. When the plot finishes the PDF is opened for you. What it produces A PDF written to your Documents folder, named drawing-layout.pdf , plotted through Print as PDF.pc3 on A3 media, millimetres, landscape, extents, centred, at 1:2. Note — Paper space only, and it needs the Print as PDF.pc3 device — same conditions as BWPDFA1 .

Sends the sheet you're on straight to the survey room printer at A3, without going through the plot dialog. How to use it Open the layout you want and run the command — there are no prompts. A message box confirms The layout "…" has been printed to "WSY-SurveyRoom". when it's done. What it produces A hard copy through the WSY-SurveyRoom.pc3 device on A3 (297 × 420 mm) media, millimetres, landscape, extents, centred, at 1:2. Nothing is added to the drawing. Note — Paper space only. If the device isn't installed the command stops before sending anything, and if the plot is cancelled or fails you get a command-line message rather than the confirmation dialog. Standards Importing the BW style set and managing annotation scales.

Replaces whatever annotation scales a drawing has accumulated with the office engineering list — the plain ratios plus the named layout scales used on engineering plan sets. It is deliberately a manual command and never runs on its own, because it wipes the list before rebuilding it. How to use it No prompts and no confirmation. It runs immediately and reports how many scales it removed and added — Scale list reset: N removed, N added. What it produces The named presets Layout Plan, Line Marking, Intersection Detail, Parking Plan, Turning 500 / 250 / 200, Sewer Layout, Water, MD Locality and MD Layout, plus the ratio scales 1:10000, 1:5000, 1:2500, 1:2000, 1:1000, 1:500, 1:250, 1:200, 1:100, 1:50, 1:25, 1:20 and 1:10. Scales that already exist by name are left alone. Note — Every other scale is removed first. The currently active scale is skipped, and any scale still referenced by annotative objects can't be deleted so it survives — but anything else you had added is gone.

Seeds a drawing with the Beveridge Williams standard styles so the engineering annotation commands have everything they need. It is the first thing to run in a drawing that didn't come from a BW template. The styles are created on demand and the full specification is re-applied every time, so a style that an older build made wrongly is repaired the next time the command runs. How to use it No prompts — run it and the styles are added. It reports [WSYDrafting] BW styles imported (BW_AN family, BWAN_DIM25/35). on the command line when it's finished. What it produces The BW_AN text-style family — BW_AN (arial narrow, annotative), BW_AN_Italics (arial italic), BW_BK_Lotno (arial black) and BW_AU (arial unicode ms) — plus the BWAN_DIM25 and BWAN_DIM35 annotative dimension styles. Note — Whatever text style, TEXTSIZE and dimension style were active before you ran it are restored afterwards, so importing the styles never changes what you're currently drawing with.

Adds annotation scales one at a time or in batches, using the office convention for metre drawings: paper units are fixed at 1 and the drawing units are the denominator divided by 1000. This is the same tool as the Add New Scale button on the WSY Drafting ribbon — it ships in the shared toolbox assembly, so both ribbons run exactly the same command. How to use it Opens a dialog rather than prompting on the command line. Enter the drawing units and a name (which auto-fills to the ratio), and add as many as you need before closing. It reports N scale(s) created. What it produces Annotation scale entries in the drawing's scale list. Nothing is drawn. A scale whose name already exists is skipped rather than duplicated. Note — Scales that arrived through an xref are hidden from the existing-names list — BricsCAD suffixes them _XREF and AutoCAD-style names contain an @ . The older prompt-based BWCSCALE has been retired; use CSCALE . Previous Command Reference

Toolbox Shared tools that ride with every plugin in the suite.

Aligns new or existing text to a polyline, arc, spline or multileader by dragging it along the target — the text rotates to follow the curve as you move, and you click to drop it. It's the tool for labelling pipes, alignments and boundaries where the label has to sit on the line. The same drag machinery is shared with the drafting ribbon's CLABEL , and the settings dialog is common to both. How to use it It loops until you exit. At Select text to align [New/Settings] <Exit>: pick existing text or mtext, choose New and answer Specify text <select>: to create some, or choose Settings to open the dialog. Then Select curve or multileader to align to: — curves nested inside blocks and xrefs are valid targets. Drag the text into place and click. Esc or Enter at the first prompt exits. The dialog controls the object type for new text (text or mtext), justification, offset factor, rotation, readable orientation, background mask and its offset, plus Multiple and Copy modes and the layer and text style used for new text. Settings persist between sessions. What it produces Moves and rotates the text you selected, or creates new text or mtext using the type, justification, layer and style set in the dialog. With Copy selected on, the original is left alone and a copy is placed; with Multiple on, it keeps dragging a fresh copy after each click. Note — Cancelling a drag restores the original text rather than leaving it half-moved. Text on a locked layer is reported as not editable and skipped.

Turns circles, ellipses and polylines into wipeouts. The native wipeout command only accepts straight-segment polylines, so this samples curved geometry into enough vertices to keep the shape. How to use it Select the objects first if you like, otherwise it asks for a selection filtered to circles, ellipses and polylines. Then Do you want to keep the original entities? [Yes/No]: , defaulting to Yes. What it produces One wipeout per valid object, on the current layer. Circles and ellipses are sampled at 50 points; polyline arc segments at 1 + 25 × √|bulge| points. It reports Wipeouts created for the selection set (N). Note — Objects that can't be sampled into at least three points are silently skipped.

Traces the outline around a set of objects. It builds a temporary rectangular frame just outside the selection's extents and then uses the native BOUNDARY command to construct outlines around every island inside that frame. This is Lee Mac's Outline Objects routine, carried in the suite's Community LISP tools component rather than compiled into the plugin. How to use it Select the objects to outline, then answer Erase original objects? [Yes/No] <Yes>: — the default erases them and leaves only the outline. What it produces One or more closed polylines or regions on the current layer, following whatever the native BOUNDARY command produces for the selection. Note — Requires the Community LISP tools component to be installed; without it the command isn't defined.

Removes every inline formatting code — colour, font, height, width, oblique, tracking, underline, overline, alignment and paragraph codes, plus stacked fractions and grouping braces — leaving plain content that picks up its appearance from the text style. It is a no-dialog strip-everything command by office preference. STRIPMTEXT is registered as an alias and does exactly the same thing. How to use it Select the objects first if you like, otherwise it asks for a selection filtered to mtext, multileaders, dimensions and block references. There are no further prompts; it reports StripMtext completed. N objects processed. What it produces Rewrites the contents of mtext, multileader mtext content, dimension text overrides and block attribute values. Mtext columns are collapsed so the text reflows as one block. Note — Line breaks ( \P ) are kept — they are content, not formatting — as are escaped literals. Stacked fractions become readable a/b text. Background masks are a property rather than an inline code, so they are left alone.

Bulk-edits a selection of annotation by putting the same string in front of or behind each item — adding units, an approx. qualifier or a diameter symbol across a set of labels in one go. How to use it Select the entities first if you like. It asks Add text as [Prefix/Suffix], defaulting to Suffix, then Text to add: (spaces allowed). If nothing was pre-selected you're then asked to Select text entities: , filtered to text, mtext and multileaders. An empty string cancels. What it produces Edits the existing entities in place; nothing is created. Note — For dimensions, a measurement with no override is represented as the <> placeholder so a prefix or suffix keeps the live measured value rather than freezing it. The engineering and drafting plugins both carry this command; the implementations are identical, so having both installed is harmless.

Constructs a polyline in model space representing what a paper space viewport actually shows, accounting for the viewport's position, scale, rotation and view direction. Useful for checking coverage before issuing a sheet set, or for building a key plan. This is Lee Mac's Viewport Outline routine, carried in the suite's Community LISP tools component. Two variants come with it: VPOL outlines every viewport in the active layout, and VPOA every viewport in every layout. How to use it Switch to a layout with no viewport active, then run it and answer Select viewport: . In model space it refuses with Command not available in Modelspace. What it produces A 2D (LW) polyline in model space tracing the transformed viewport boundary. Rectangular, polygonal and clipped viewports are all handled, including arc segments. Note — Requires the Community LISP tools component. The polyline's properties and optional interior offset are fixed in that routine's own parameters section. Previous Command Reference

What each one does, what it asks you, what it draws and anything worth knowing before you run it. Search commands Or press / anywhere on the site. Prefer to browse? The ribbon tabs are below, and the full alphabetical list is at the bottom.
Commands without a ribbon button Office-tool commands typed at the command line.

Adds lot labels to boundaries that the lot loader brought in earlier — useful when you imported without labels, deleted some, or want them back after tidying up. It reads the plan details from the xdata the loader attached rather than going back to the web service. How to use it Select the lot boundaries first if you like, otherwise it asks to Select lots to label: , filtered to polylines. It reports [NSWLotLoader] Applied labels to N lot(s). What it produces One MText per lot at an interior point of the boundary, middle-centre at 1.0 height, holding the lot number, section number and plan label on separate lines. Boundaries on SUB BDY are labelled onto SUB DP (yellow); everything else goes onto ADJ DP (white). The layers are created if they don't exist. Note — It only works on polylines carrying NSW_PARCEL xdata — boundaries drawn by hand or brought in another way are silently skipped. It doesn't check whether a lot is already labelled, so running it twice on the same selection doubles the labels up. There is no ribbon button; type the command. Previous Command Reference
Tools The NSW Lot Loader and Point Cloud Digitizer.

Opens the lot loader, which pulls cadastral boundaries, lot labels, road names and road centrelines straight from the NSW Spatial service into model space. Lots can be found by lot and plan number, by picking a point, or by an extent. The panel is modeless, so it stays open while you work in the drawing. The ? button in its title bar opens offline help. How to use it The command itself has no prompts — it just shows the panel, and everything happens in the form. Set the import options (subject and adjoining lot labels, road names, road centrelines), choose one of the three searches, and click Fetch Lots . Entries and settings are remembered for next time. What it produces Polylines and MText on the office cadastral layers: SUB BDY and SUB DP for the lots you asked for, ADJ BDY and ADJ DP for neighbours and the surrounding buffer, ROAD NAME and ROAD CL for roads. The By Point and By Extent searches put everything on the ADJ layers. Lots already loaded are skipped rather than duplicated. Each boundary carries the parcel details as NSW_PARCEL xdata. Note — It needs internet access to the NSW Spatial service. The MGA zone is worked out from the fetched data; if it can't be determined the tool assumes Zone 56 and says so in the status bar — worth checking on a Zone 55 job.

Shows or hides the digitizer panel, which traces features off a point cloud — stepping along at a fixed distance per vertex, or tracing freely — with every vertex snapped to the cloud, numbered and coded as it goes. Each drawing gets its own panel. The panel's buttons run the companion commands: PCDIG_LINE (Add Line), PCDIG_POINT (Add Point), PCDIG_EXTEND (Extend an existing 3D polyline) and PCDIG_EXPORT (Export to 12da). How to use it The command itself has no prompts — it toggles the panel. Set the segment distance, point numbering, point code and layer (manually or from a Trimble .fxl feature library) in the panel, then start a run. Digitising prompts Pick point (Esc to exit): with an Undo keyword that steps back a vertex; Extend asks you to Select polyline near the end you wish to extend: . What it produces 3D polylines and, optionally, survey points on the feature's layer — Civil points where the Civil module is available, otherwise standard points with the number and code attached. The layer is created from the feature library's colour if it doesn't exist. Export to 12da… writes the digitised strings and points to a 12d Model ASCII file. Note — While digitising, 2D object snaps are turned off and point-cloud nearest snapping is turned on, and PDMODE / PDSIZE are set for point visibility if they were at their defaults — all restored when the run ends. A locked target layer stops the run before it starts. The export can't run while a digitising run is active. Previous Command Reference
Annotations WAE text, grades, comments and the certification tick.

Writes the office certification paragraph in full, with the registered surveyor's name and the surface layer filled in — the block of text that goes on the front sheet of every WAE set. How to use it Three prompts: Select Surveyor [Ben/Angela/Peter]: , which expands to the surveyor's full registered name; Select Surface type [First/Second/fInal]: , the AC layer the road centrelines were taken on; then Specify point to place text: . What it produces One MText block 150 units wide at 2.5 height in the WAE LABEL style, on layer ANNOTATIONS . It covers the work-as-executed certification, interallotment drainage within easements, the road centreline layer, Australian Height Datum, and pit and pipe sizes being as per design — followed by a signature rule and a line reading ADD DATE AND COMMENTS HERE . Note — The surveyor list is fixed in the command. A name that isn't on it has to be typed over afterwards.

Computes a grade from two levels and a distance and places the result as a labelled percentage, so pipe and road grades can be annotated straight off the surveyed levels without a calculator. How to use it It loops so you can do several in a row. For each grade: Select first level or press Enter to input manually: — pick a text entity and the first number in it is read out, or press Enter and answer Enter first level: . The same for the second level. Then Choose chainage method [Direct/Calculate]: — Direct asks Enter chainage directly: , Calculate asks for a first and second length and uses the absolute difference, echoing what it worked out. Finally Specify point to place <grade> grade text: , with the computed value already shown in the prompt. Esc finishes. What it produces MText at 2.5 height, middle-centre, in the WAE LABEL style on layer ANNOTATIONS , reading the grade to one decimal place with a percent sign — for example 1.5% . The calculation is (first level − second level) ÷ chainage × 100. Note — A chainage of zero is rejected — it says Chainage cannot be zero. and starts the cycle again rather than failing. A selected text with no number in it gives Invalid selection, try again.

Fixes annotation that has ended up upside down — usually after a marked-up sheet has been rotated. Rotating about the middle centre means the text stays where it was rather than swinging away from the feature it labels. How to use it Select the text first if you like, otherwise it asks for a selection filtered to text and mtext. No further prompts; it reports Text flipped 180 degrees with Middle Center attachment. What it produces Edits the selected entities in place: attachment or justification is set to middle centre and the rotation is increased by 180°. Note — The justification change is permanent, so flipping twice returns the text to its original angle but not to its original justification.

Quick annotation on a WAE sheet at a fixed horizontal rotation, so you can letter a rotated or imported sheet without fighting the UCS or the drawing's angle base. How to use it Run it, answer Text insertion point: , then type the text in place and finish as normal. Because the WAE LABEL style has a fixed height you are never asked for one. What it produces Single-line text at 0°, top-left justified, on layer ANNOTATIONS in the WAE LABEL style (Lucida Sans Unicode, fixed 2.5 height — not annotative, because WAE sheets are worked at paper scale). Colour, linetype and lineweight are set ByLayer. Note — ANGBASE is temporarily zeroed so the text lands at a true 0° whatever the drawing's angle base is, then restored when the text command ends.

Bulk-edits marked-up annotation by adding the same string to the front or the back of each selected item. How to use it Select the text first if you like, otherwise it asks for a selection filtered to text, mtext and multileaders. Then Choose [Prefix/Suffix]: and Enter text for Prefix/Suffix: (spaces allowed). It reports Modification completed. What it produces Edits the selected entities in place; nothing is created. Multileaders are only edited when their content is mtext. Note — This is the WAE ribbon's own command. The engineering and drafting ribbons carry TADD , which does the same job and also handles dimension text.

The vertical companion to HTXT — for labelling down the side of a sheet or along a vertical feature. How to use it Run it, answer Text insertion point: , then type the text in place. No height prompt — the WAE label style has a fixed height. What it produces Single-line text at 270°, top-left justified, on layer ANNOTATIONS in the WAE LABEL style at its fixed 2.5 height. Note — Like HTXT , it zeroes ANGBASE for the placement and restores it afterwards.

Drops the standard WAE tick — the mark used to sign off items checked against the design — as many times as you need in one run. How to use it Run it and answer Specify insertion point: for each tick. It keeps asking until you press Esc. What it produces Block references of the waetick block on layer ANNOTATIONS , with colour, linetype and lineweight ByLayer. The block definition is imported from Support\waetick.dwg beside the plugin on first use and reused afterwards. Note — If the block drawing is missing you get [BW WAE] waetick.dwg not found beside the plugin — reinstall the WAE component. Previous Command Reference
Sheeting Bringing the design sheet into the Works-As-Executed drawing.

Turns a folder of scanned or exported design sheets into a set of layouts — one per image, named after the file, with the image stretched to fill the sheet and the page already set up to plot. This is the starting point for a works-as-executed job: import the design sheets, then mark them up in red. How to use it Run it and answer Specify sheet size [A4/A3/A2/A1]: — Enter takes the A1 default. A file dialog opens (at the drawing's Rasters folder if there is one) where you can select many images at once. If some of them already have layouts you're asked once, N of the selected sheet(s) already have layouts [Replace/Skip]: , defaulting to Skip. Progress is reported per sheet and it finishes on the first layout it created. What it produces A layout per image, its default viewport erased and the raster attached on the SHEET layer, stretched to the paper size. Each layout is configured for Print As PDF.pc3 at the chosen media, millimetres, rotated 90°, centred, plot type extents, with the BW_FINAL.ctb plot style table shown, and opens zoomed to extents. Note — The whole import is one undo group — a single U removes every layout it made. Characters that layout names can't hold are replaced with hyphens, and a file whose name leaves nothing usable is skipped. Drafting Standards Why we draw the way we do — the conventions that make our drawings consistent, legible and plottable. Whose standards these are. This is Western Sydney drafting practice , written down — not a firm-wide mandate. The tools work in any office; these conventions are what we draw to. Standardising across the business is the direction we'd like to head, and this exists so there's something concrete to compare against. If your office does something differently and the difference matters, tell us .

Line weight carries meaning: boundaries read heavier than annotation, and easements read lighter still. We drive weight from colour through the plot style table rather than setting it per object, so weight stays consistent no matter who drew the object.

A small set of named styles covers everything, each sized for a role — large for lot numbers, medium for areas, small for dimensions and bearings, thin for labels. Using the named styles rather than ad-hoc heights is what keeps a drawing coherent.

Every object belongs on a layer that describes what it is , not what it looks like. The ribbon commands create and set the correct layer for you. Keep drawings tidy with DWGHEALTH and PURGE before issuing.

Nearly all our text and symbols are annotative: they're defined once and displayed at the correct size for whatever annotation scale a viewport uses. This is what lets one model space serve sheets at different scales. Note — set the annotation scale before placing annotative objects. Objects only display at the scales attached to them.
Plot styles map colour to line weight. Page setups are configured per sheet size, and the plot commands apply the correct device and style table for you.

Where a plan is rotated in a viewport, annotation should read horizontally on the sheet. Commands that place text account for the viewport twist and the current UCS. Previous Using the Ribbon Next WSY Drafting Standards

Introduction to BricsCAD BricsCAD is the CAD package the office draws in. If you've used AutoCAD you'll find it immediately familiar — same commands, same file format, same way of working.

Survey data comes in from the field, is processed, and arrives as points, strings and surfaces. From there the work diverges — a plan drafted and annotated to our standards, a Works-As-Executed set marked up against the design, an engineering detail dimensioned and plotted — but it all passes through BricsCAD and it all goes out as PDF. The plugin suite exists to make that middle step fast and consistent, whichever of those you're doing.

BricsCAD uses the same DWG format, so files move between the two without conversion. Command names, aliases and the general interface are close enough that most habits carry over directly. The differences you're most likely to notice are in the settings dialogs and some of the more specialised toolsets.

Not everyone works in BricsCAD. Survey processing and design work often happen in other packages, and drawings arrive as exports from those. It's worth knowing what a file has been through before you start editing it.

Drawing Checklist A QA panel over the office checklist spreadsheet. It tracks one pass per drawing revision, and can check and fix a few drawing settings directly.

Run OPENCHECKLIST , or use the Checklist button on the WSY Drafting ribbon's QA panel. The drawing must be saved — the checklist lives with the project, and its location is worked out from the drawing's folder. If the project doesn't have a checklist yet, one is created from the office master template.

Job details at the top fill themselves in from the drawing name where they can. Tick Done or N/A for each task — they're mutually exclusive, and completed tasks grey out. Space toggles the focused task. Right-click for bulk actions: complete a section, complete everything remaining, or clear all. Category rows have their own tick boxes that set every task beneath them.

Each drawing revision gets its own QA pass. Use the Revision dropdown to switch between them, and + Add revision to start a new one. Note — a new revision only exists in memory until you press Save checklist . If you switch revisions with unticked changes you'll be asked whether to keep them, discard them, or stay put.

A few items check the drawing themselves and offer to fix it: Item Checks Fix UCS orientation The UCS is World and the view isn't twisted Set to World — resets the UCS, straightens the view and zooms to the drawing Drawing units Units are metres Set metres North point Every layout has a north point Go to layout — jumps to the first sheet missing one The first two are authoritative: their ticks follow the drawing, so they can't be ticked by hand and then drift out of true. The north point check is advisory — some sheets genuinely don't need one — so you can still tick it yourself. Checks re-run whenever the window regains focus, so fixing something in the drawing updates the panel straight away.

Save checklist writes back to the spreadsheet and records who checked it and when. The panel stays open. If the file is open in Excel you'll be asked to close it and retry. Closing a drawing — if the project has a checklist, you'll be asked whether to complete it before the drawing closes. Previous Quality Next Onboarding

Troubleshooting For the whole suite — any ribbon tab, any tool. Nearly everything is fixed by reinstalling, so start there and only work down the list if it persists.

This fixes most problems, and it is safe: uninstalling reverses exactly what the installer did — it removes the plugins, the office alias it added to your alias file, and any profile it created, and it puts back the profile you were using before. Your drawings are never touched. Close BricsCAD. It writes its settings back when it exits, so uninstalling underneath it leaves the old registrations behind. Open Windows Settings › Apps › Installed apps , find BW BricsCAD Tools , and choose Uninstall . Install it again from the install page — always take the current version rather than an installer you saved earlier. Start BricsCAD. The ribbons load themselves. Searching Installed apps for “BW BricsCAD Tools”, then … › Uninstall . Click to enlarge. Reinstalling is not how you update. Updates install themselves — you'll get a small bubble in the corner, and the update applies next time you close BricsCAD. Reinstall only to fix something that's broken. To force an update now, type WSYUPDATE .

Restart BricsCAD first — ribbons load at startup, and a tab can be missed if BricsCAD was busy. If it is still missing, the usual cause is that the component isn't installed: each ribbon is optional, so a machine set up for Drafting has no BW Engineering tab. Reinstall and tick the discipline you need. If the tab is still absent after a clean reinstall, the customisation may be holding a stale menu group. Run CUSTOMIZE , find the group in Manage Your Customizations and unload it, then restart BricsCAD so the plugin loads it fresh.

That part of the suite isn't installed. Everything is optional at install time, so commands only exist if their component was ticked: If this fails You need OPENCHECKLIST The Drawing Checklist component NSWLOTS The NSW Lot Loader component PCDIG The Point Cloud Digitizer component OUTLINE / VPO The Community LISP tools component Engineering or WAE commands The matching discipline — Engineering or Surveying Run the installer again and tick the discipline that carries it. The wizard remembers what you chose last time, so you are adding to your setup, not starting over. For an individual component rather than a whole discipline, tick Advanced on the first page and choose it from the component list.
